title: Ch-S-D
hookLine: chesed (kindness) and chasid, the kind one

cards: A tall white bird with long legs and a long bill, standing on a rooftop nest. In the list of birds in Leviticus, the stork is called the chasidah.

The Talmud stops to ask why a bird would carry that name, and answers simply: because she does chesed with her companions, sharing her food. A bird named for kindness, tucked into a list that's easy to skim.
It holds today's root, found from the Psalms to the book of Ruth, and a name a whole movement within Judaism would one day take for itself.

teach.h: CHESED: LOVE THAT KEEPS SHOWING UP.
teach.b: Ch-S-D. Chet, samech, dalet. Four ways in.
First, chesed: kindness, loving-kindness, steadfast love. English keeps reaching for it and never quite fits. A Psalm repeats one refrain line after line: "For His mercy endureth for ever."
Mercy there is chesed. In these texts it's loyalty that goes beyond what's required, love that keeps showing up. Second, chesed between people.
In the book of Ruth, Naomi blesses her two widowed daughters-in-law: "the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me." Dealt kindly is chesed.

Their husbands were gone, and they had kept faith with her anyway. A few verses on, Ruth refuses to leave her. And the prophet Micah asks what is required, and answers: "to do justly, and to love mercy."
Justice, from yesterday, with chesed beside it. Third, the chasid.
In Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the sages, someone who says what's mine is yours, and what's yours is yours, is called a chasid: the kind one, who gives past the line.
The same sayings teach that the world stands on three things, and one is acts of loving-kindness. Fourth, the name.
Hasidim, a movement within Judaism, take their name from this root.
Before it was a movement, it was a description: someone whose kindness overflows. Tzedakah gives what's owed. Chesed gives what isn't.

how: Jewish tradition counts gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness such as visiting the sick, comforting mourners and hosting guests, as a pillar of the world; Hasidic Jews take their name from the word chasid.

games.q: you're Naomi. your sons have died, and you tell your two widowed daughters-in-law to go home. what word do you use for how they've treated you and the dead?
games.why: chesed. Naomi blesses them because they dealt kindly, with chesed, with the dead and with her.

practice: Bring to mind one person you'll see or talk to soon, and something kind you could do for them that you don't owe: a word of praise they won't expect, a door held a few seconds longer, food shared the way the stork does.
Picture yourself doing it, notice whatever comes up at the thought, and let it settle. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Ch-S-D. Chet, samech, dalet: the root of chesed, loving-kindness; chasid, the kind one; and chasidah, the stork. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: loving-kindness, love that goes past what's required.

carryVoice: Your line: a hasid is kind. Kindness nobody is owed is still kindness worth giving. See you soon.
